rewriteLast.title: Chapter 5 · The Burglar in the Nursery
rewriteLast.artPrompt: a dark nursery at night where a golden bird blazes like a bonfire with wings spread wide, a startled burglar in a black jersey dropping a small shaded lantern, four children in nightgowns sitting up in bed, a baby's cot in the corner, warm fierce golden light against deep blue shadows, dramatic but gentle storybook illustration

blocks.text: One night a man crept up the stairs of the quiet house, soft as a shadow. The house was dark, and the town clock struck one. He had heard that the children kept strange treasures, and strange treasures bring money. He tried the nursery door. Inside, four children slept, and the baby in his cot. On the hearth-rug, wrapped in its own golden glow, lay the Phoenix.
The Phoenix wakes and blazes, and the burglar wishes he were anywhere else.

The Phoenix did not sing at all that time. It rose up like a bonfire, wings wide, and filled the whole nursery with light. The hall clock, the flower-pots, and the umbrella-stand all lit up gold. Its eyes were two small suns. "WHO COMES HERE?" it said, and every letter of its voice was on fire. The burglar dropped his dark lantern, tumbled down the stairs, and was caught by the constable at the garden gate.
New word: constable - a policeman. This one was very surprised to catch a burglar running out of a quiet, peaceful house.

But when the children saw the man's thin face, they could not help being sorry for him. He looked colder than the night itself. "He only came because he was hungry and unlucky," said Anthea. So they carried out bread and cold mutton and a great jug of tea. The constable, who was a kind man, let them stand it all on the step.

The burglar ate as if he had not eaten for a week. Then he wiped his eyes with his cuff. "I'll go straight, Missies," he said. "See if I don't." The children went back to bed feeling taller than usual. And the Phoenix hummed a small golden song on the stairs all night. It sounded like a kettle singing about second chances.

chapters.title: Chapter 6 · A Hundred Tired Clerks
chapters.artPrompt: an Edwardian nursery crowded with a hundred solemn clerks in paper collars and bowler hats standing in neat rows with umbrellas, four children and a baby looking up in astonishment, a golden bird singing from the fireplace fender, warm lamplight, funny cozy storybook illustration

blocks.text: "Let us spend one wish on other people," said Anthea. "Doing good is better than getting things." They thought of the pale, tired clerks they saw each morning pouring out of the trains. A hundred of them, at least, hurried to their desks with hungry eyes and paper collars. The wish came out before anyone could weigh it. "We wish," said Cyril grandly, "that the poor tired clerks could have one perfectly happy day."
The carpet has brought a hundred clerks - and the nursery is very full.

The carpet heard. That evening the nursery was absolutely full of clerks. There were a hundred of them at least, standing in rows with their umbrellas. Every chair was filled, and so was every corner. "We are at your service," said the eldest clerk. The children looked at the beds, the toy-cupboard, and one another. A hundred clerks do not fit into any nursery in England.
Talk together: The children wished for a good thing and got far more of it than they meant. What should they have said more carefully?

Then the children worked like beavers all evening. The Phoenix gave the clerks a song, and the cook carried up bread and cheese until midnight. The eldest clerk made a speech about the kindness of children. In the morning the carpet carried all one hundred clerks away to the sea-side for their happy day. It brought them home again by dusk, sandy, merry, and scarlet, every one.

The clerks thanked the children as if they had done it all on purpose. The baby clapped his hands at all the shiny boots. "It was a muddle," said Anthea honestly, on the way up to bed. "But it was a kind muddle," said the Phoenix from the fender. And that, it said, is the best kind of muddle to learn from.

chapters.title: Chapter 7 · The Fireworks Fair
chapters.artPrompt: a night fair on a common with a huge firework display of green and gold rockets, a splendid golden bird flying among the sparks singing, upturned faces of a cheering crowd below, four children watching from a flying carpet in the air, glowing embers and deep blue night, joyful magical storybook illustration

blocks.text: There was to be a fair on the common, with a great firework display at nine o'clock. The Phoenix begged to go. "Fire," it said, "is my oldest friend. Yet I have never seen it dressed in colors." The Phoenix had never been so excited in five hundred years. So after supper the children folded up the carpet, and the whole family flew off over the sleeping town. The Phoenix rode above them like a small golden flame.
The Phoenix sings among the rockets, brighter than every firework in the sky.

The fair was all lamps and merry-go-rounds and sugar-stick smells. Then the first rocket went up with a scream and burst into green and gold. The Phoenix rose at once to meet it. It flew among the fireworks, singing its golden song, spiraling and flashing. Even the band stopped to watch. The crowd below pointed and shouted that never, never had there been such a display.
Question for you: The crowd thinks the Phoenix is part of the show. Is it funny or lonely to be wonderful when nobody knows who you are?

"They are cheering me," said the Phoenix, and its feathers stood up with pride. It flew higher, and sang louder, and outshone the finest rocket of the night. The children below grew a little quiet. They were glad for their friend. Cyril held Jane's hand tight in the dark. And yet they remembered that the Phoenix was made of fire, and that fire, one day, comes home.

They flew home over the dark fields with the sparks still drifting behind them. The Phoenix perched on the nursery fender and looked long into the coals. Its song, that night, was very soft. "Not yet," it said, though nobody had asked. "Not quite yet." The children said good night very gently, as if the Phoenix were asleep.

chapters.title: Chapter 8 · The Hole in the Carpet
chapters.artPrompt: an old Turkish carpet spread out on a nursery floor in daytime light, a round burnt hole in its middle and fraying edges, four children kneeling around it examining it gravely, a golden bird perched on the fender watching, one child measuring the hole with a ruler, soft afternoon light, gentle storybook illustration

blocks.text: The carpet was beginning to show its age. The old burn from the fireworks had left a round hole in its very middle. The edges, too, were going, fray by fray. Robert measured the hole with his ruler, and it had grown since spring. "A carpet with a hole in it," said Mother, "will soon have to be made into door-mats." The children looked at one another in horror. Door-mats do not fly. They kept quiet and did not explain why.
The old carpet is wearing out, fray by fray, like all wonderful things.

That afternoon they spread the carpet out and examined it like doctors. The hole was honest and round, and the fringes were thinning. "Magic is wearing out with the wool," said the Phoenix gently. "A carpet cannot fly for ever, little ones. Nothing can - except stories." The children were silent, for they knew it was true.
Talk together: Mother sees an old carpet with a hole. The children see a magic carpet. How can both of them be right?

So they made a resolution, the four of them together. While the carpet still had flying in it, every flight should count. No more careless wishes, no more rushing off to anywhere. They would choose one last journey, the finest of them all. Even the baby seemed to understand, and laughed at the word "resolution". And they would take the baby, who had never flown at all.

"And where shall it be?" whispered Jane. But the Phoenix only preened its golden feathers and looked into the fire. "The best journeys," it said, "like the best songs, should be saved for the end." The children went to bed full of the whole world to choose from. And the Phoenix hummed a little golden song about endings.

chapters.title: Chapter 9 · The Last Flight
chapters.artPrompt: a worn patterned carpet flying steady and low over a golden sunset sea, five children and a baby in a shawl aboard, a golden bird sailing above with feathers burning like a small sun, waves turned to gold to the edge of the world, gulls and first stars, warm glowing storybook illustration

blocks.text: They chose at last, and chose together, the way good families do. "The sea at sunset," said Anthea, "where we were so cold and miserable before. Let us see it kind this time." So on a golden evening the carpet rose from the nursery window with all five of them aboard. The baby was tucked in the middle, in a shawl, with biscuits. The Phoenix sailed above like a small flame.
The carpet carries them over the sunset sea, and this time nothing goes wrong.

This time the sea was kind. The sun went down slow and red, and the waves ran gold to the very edge of the world. The carpet hung in the warm air as steady as a floor. The Phoenix's feathers burned like a little sun in the red light. The baby laughed at the gulls. Nobody was cold, nobody was frightened. The Phoenix sang its whole long song, from the first verse to the last.
Question for you: The children return to the place that once went wrong. Why does going back and setting things right feel so good?

They stayed until the stars came out. Then the carpet bore them home gently, like a leaf settling on water. The house welcomed them with the smell of supper. "Thank you, old friend," said Cyril, patting the worn wool. The carpet, though it could not speak, seemed to gather them up more carefully than usual. It was as if it too were saying good-bye.

That night the Phoenix stood on the nursery fender a long time, looking into the coals. The coals sank and glowed, and glowed again, like a heart. "I am five hundred years old," it said at last. "And my year is ending. Soon, little ones - very soon now." And the children lay awake a long while in the dark, saying nothing at all.

chapters.title: Chapter 10 · The Egg in the Fire
chapters.artPrompt: a nursery hearth at night where a single great golden egg lies warm among soft ashes on a fold of an old worn carpet, four children kneeling round it with wondering faces, the firelight glowing rose and gold, deep blue night outside the window, tender magical storybook illustration

blocks.text: The Phoenix chose its own night, and it chose the fireworks fair. The sky over the common was clear, and the air smelled of autumn. "If a Phoenix must end," it said, "let it end in glory, among colors, with people looking up." The children held it close, one by one, and did not try to keep it. Their eyes were wet, but their voices were steady.
Where the Phoenix burned, a golden egg lies warm in the nursery ashes.

It flew up into the burst and blaze of the display, higher than any rocket. It sang its golden song with all its breath. Every rocket seemed to bow to it as it passed. Then it folded its wings and became one with its own fire - a star among stars, a spark among sparks. The crowd cheered the finest display of their lives. And they never knew.
Talk together: The Phoenix must burn to be born again. How can letting something go be part of loving it?

But the Phoenix had left them something. When the children knelt at the nursery fire, there in the warm ashes lay a single great egg. It was gold as morning, and warm as a heart. Jane put her warm hands round it, and it glowed brighter. "In two thousand years," said Cyril softly, "there will be a new Phoenix. And the egg is safe with us."

They kept the egg on a fold of the old carpet, in the warmest corner of the fender. Mother supposed it to be a harmless ornament. The carpet saw out its days as a nursery rug, worn and holey and beloved. And sometimes, when the fire burned low, the egg glowed - very softly. It seemed as if something inside it were dreaming of wings.
